description: The Sparks is a student-led team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We are passionate about AI, Machine Learning, Python, Data Science, and space exploration. For the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, we aim to analyze scientific data, study lunar terrain, identify potential landing sites and hazards, and present findings through interactive maps. Through teamwork, research, and innovation, we hope to develop a useful solution for future space exploration.
summary:
We built ASTRO, a web app for exploring how sunlight and Earth visibility differ between two lunar south-pole locations: Nobile Rim 1 and Nobile Rim 2. Choose a date and time range, then see the Sun and Earth’s positions compared with the local terrain skyline. ASTRO combines saved JPL Horizons data with LOLA-based terrain profiles, so the comparison works offline.

The app estimates visibility by checking whether the center of the Sun or Earth is above the modeled skyline at each sampled time. This helps users see how nearby ridges and timing can affect what is visible. ASTRO is an early screening and learning tool, not a landing-site recommendation. It does not calculate solar power, assess landing safety, or confirm a working communications link. It is an independent project and is not endorsed by NASA.
details:
ASTRO is an offline-first web app by The Sparks for comparing how terrain affects sunlight and Earth line of sight at two lunar south-pole reference points: Nobile Rim 1 and Nobile Rim 2. Users select a supported UTC date and time window, switch between sites, and view Sun and Earth directions against a locally modeled terrain skyline. The app combines a seven-day JPL Horizons time series with LOLA-derived terrain profiles. At each sampled time, a body’s center is counted as visible when its elevation is above the skyline in that direction.

ASTRO helps students, educators, and early mission-planning discussions explore how location, time, terrain, and sky geometry relate. Its creative contribution is an explainable offline comparison, not a new scientific model. We used HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Node.js, and bundled JSON data; no special hardware is required. We considered terrain coverage, 10-minute sampling, frame alignment, and the difference between geometric visibility and operational capability. The terrain radius is 10 km; the app does not estimate power, landing safety, or radio-link availability. AI tools assisted with planning, research, coding and debugging, and writing. The presentation cover includes AI-generated concept art, not scientific data. ASTRO itself has no AI model and is not endorsed by NASA.
